speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
It will be within the memory of at least some members of the house that expropriation proceedings were taken at the point where the Hudson Bay railway entered Churchill. A description of the land by metes and bounds was made by engineers. The department know nothing about the owners. They file the plan thus prepared by engineers. Then the appropriate searches are made and notices given to all the persons affected. Tenders are made of the money which it is believed will be fair compensation for the land thus taken. The first step is the preparation of the plan by metes and bounds which describes the area; I want to make that clear. When that is done the plan is filed. When the plan is filed no one knows better than does the senior member for Ottawa, that it goes to the registry office. In the registry office search is made by the solicitors in charge of the expropriation proceedings; notice is given to the people concerned and a tender is made. If they decline to accept the sum offered, then proceedings are instituted in the exchequer court. If they get more than was tendered, they receive the costs of the proceedings, and if they get less, the costs are deducted from the tender made. That is the case here. I recall the circumstances in connection with the order in council. It contains merely a description of the land with a plan attached showing the area involved in order that proceedings might be taken promptly so that there might be no speculation worked. The question was litigated whether Mr. Dunning as Minister of Railways had power to file that
Supply-National Defence

plan while certain proceedings were pending, and it will be recalled that in Montreal before any action was taken with respect to the tunnel there, the Minister of Railways filed his plan. That plan was for the purpose of vesting the properties in the crown in the right of the railway company, in this case vesting these properties in the crown. My information is that it is expected that from the proceeds of the sale of these lands the moneys paid for them will be fully repaid, because it is to carry a road through connecting with the Montreal highway, and will provide additional building sites which the departmental officials believe will more than compensate the government for the initial payment to be made. And the provision is made that the moneys thus received shall be paid into the consolidated revenue fund, and not to the federal district commission. So that the crown will be reimbursed the money which it now temporarily advances. .

I do not know what information the Prime Minister had in regard to the expropriation of lands for the Hudson Bay railway, but I cannot conceive of anything different happening in Manitoba from what would happen in any other province. In other provinces when lands are expropriated for a railway, before the expropriation can take place a plan must be filed by the railway company showing how much land is taken and how much is taken from each owner; the names of the owners must be on the plan, and that plan must be filed with the registrar of deeds in the district. So if my right hon. friend got the information in connection with the Hudson Bay railway that there were no names of owners of land on the plan, presumably the land belonged to the crown; consequently the Prime Minister in making that argument is not fair to the committee. In regard to the expropriation of lands outside of railways I have also had some experience, and I say to the Prime Minister-great lawyer as he is-that before expropriation proceedings take place the plan must be filed, showing the names of owners and acreage of each owner. It is useless for the Prime Minister to try to tell this committee anything else, and we are not going to take such an answer. We want the names of the owners of the land indicated on the plan or else this item will be held up.

I must correct the hon.
gentleman. The Expropriation Act is the act at issue here, not the Railway Act. When I spoke of what took place at Churchill I was

pointing out that the Minister of Railways filed a plan as he did in connection with the taking in Montreal. I was not saying what the plan contained; I merely say he filed a plan and the lands were thereupon set apart. So far as this is concerned the lands are vested in the crown by reason of the filing of the plan and the taking possession.

The plan must contain the
name3 of the owners.

that has to be done, because they may not be known. That is a matter that arises after the solicitors take charge of the expropriation proceedings. The Railway Act is one thing, the Expropriation Act another. There is no reason for any heat or anger about this matter. I investigated the matter for my own satisfaction as I do matters of this kind generally, and what happened I have explained. The area of land is described by metes and bounds. The plan is filed, the land is vested in the crown, and the crown may then take possession. I remember on that plan there was the name of someone, Eagleson, I think as the suggested owner of the property.

The plan shows the names of Eagleson, James Fox and another Fox- two Foxes, several names; but there is no indication as far as the plan goes of the amounts of land being purchased from each of those owners.

The Prime Minister need not try to insinuate that there is anger on this side; and the only heat, if there is heat, is caused by himself. We had to adjourn this house for five weeks and go home and come back here in the middle of summer, and he ought, to appreciate our being willing to do it. Here to-night we are sweating in this hot chamber when this house ought to be prorogued and we all ought to be home. And the quicker we get out of this the better, let me say to the Prime Minister, for his own sake and the sake of everyone else. The only other heat was in New Brunswick to-day, the Prime Minister's own province, which elected forty-three Liberals and only five Conservatives.
Hear, hear.

If the heat has affected the
Prime Minister in any way it has not affected us, except that we realize that the people of this country want a federal election at the earliest moment.
As regards expropriation proceedings, I have had something to do with them in connection both with railways and with other lands, and

I say to the Prime Minister that before a government or anyone else can expropriate property they must file a plan with the registrar of deeds and the names of the owners of the land must appear on that plan.

May I ask the minister who initiated these proceedings?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Perhaps I may be permitted to say a, word. This whole scheme was initiated in the first place by the federal district commission. I may not be accurate as to whether it preceded the defence or air service but I know that over a long period of time the federal district commission have been extremely anxious to get an eastern entrance to the city of Ottawa via the driveway. They are making a very beautiful entrance to this city which, apart altogether from the beautification, will have the effect of relieving congestion on the Montreal road in years to come, leaving the road through Eastview for the heavier traffic.
So far as the air force is concerned, I have had occasion to fly from that field a number of times, and in discussing the matter with members of the air force I have found that they always have been very nervous about the high hill on the south side that is covered with tall trees. You must land on a flying field in conformity with the wind that is blowing at the time, and if a landing has to be effected from the south side there is very grave danger because of that high hill and the trees upon it. The air force always have been very nervous with respect to that physical condition and have wanted the shoulder of that hill removed so that the menace might be eliminated. This dovetails into the scheme of the Ottawa Improvement Commission. I speak of these facts because I have had occasion to discuss the matter with the federal district commission several times, and the view I have ex-

pressed as to the air force came to me incidentally from the different officers with whom I have had contact.

If that is the case why smuggle the item in under the head of engineering services and works? There are separate items for aviation under which this amount might more properly be placed. Why not put it under the federal district commission?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I shall not quarrel with my right hon. friend, but there was no question of attempting to hide the item. I think it is a most praiseworthy step; I think it is in the public interest, and I believe that in the years to come it will return a much larger sum of money than will be expended on it. It might have been better to put it under a separate item, but it touches three different departments and the engineering branch of the Department of National Defence naturally would do the surveying. I assume that is why it appears in a national defence item, but there was no attempt or intention to disguise the item. I should think my right hon. friend, who always has been an advocate of the beautlncation oi Ottawa-aiiu I say this in his praise-would ibe the first to say that this undertaking is one designed in a marked degree to enhance the beauty of Ottawa. At the same time it will serve another purpose; it will provide more satisfactory accommodation for the Department of Justice in connection wtih the mounted police and will round out- a proper landing field for the capital city of Canada.

I may say to my hon, friend that I would be the first to support him and the government in any soheme that would meet the two necessities of which he has spoken and at the same time help in a necessary civic improvement, but the last place I would expect to find it would be in the most unpopular vote that is presented to this house, namely, an increase in the vote for militia services. I wonder very much that the government should have selected this particular service to cover the purchase of this property. So far as the land is concerned, in connection with the purposes mentioned by my hon. friend, I am quite prepared to withdraw my objection to the purchase, but this is a very different explanation from the one given by the Minister of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If there had been any intention on the part of the government to smuggle this vote into the estimates, certainly

Supply-National Defence
the government went about it in a very clumsy fashion. As my right hon. friend has suggested, this amount could have been put in a separate item, and to that extent it would have reduced the militia estimates and lessened the criticism of military expenditures.
Just another mistake by the government.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may say to my hon. friend from Antigonish-Guysborough -that the government has made many mistakes. I have not known of a government in the history of Canada that has not made many mistakes, and I never expect to see a government of Canada that will not make mistakes. I suggest to my hon. friend that the government that does not make mistakes does not make anything. We would be the first to admit that we have made mistakes, but certainly if this is a mistake it must ibe apparent that it was not done with any sinister purpose.

With what the Minister of Finance has said with reference to improving the approach to Ottawa I have no quarrel whatever, because that matter has been mooted for a long time. Undoubtedly there must be a further approach from the east in order to relieve the congestion of traffic on the Montreal road and also to meet the objection to the landing field at Rockcliffe. That is nothing new; that has been talked of for three, four or five years, ever since the inception of that aviation field. We all agree that better landing facilities should be provided and that the congestion on the Montreal road should be relieved; with that I have no quarrel at all, but there have been many alternatives proposed. For a long time the local newspapers have been advocating an entrance from the east, but this is not the only alternative. I must agree with what my right hon. leader has stated; if this vote had been properly put in the estimates those who are primarily interested in following these matters would have had some knowledge of it. It was purely and simply a matter of luck, or perhaps a matter of psychology, that in considering the estimates this matter came up; otherwise no one would have known anything about it- until the whole thing had been completed. To that procedure I must register strenuous opposition. It was not fair to the people of Ottawa; it was not fair to the representatives of the people of Ottawa in this parliament that a matter such as this should have been contemplated and practically
consummated without anyone having the slightest knowledge that the project was under way. That is why I feel that the matter has not been handled in the fairest way.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: My colleague the Minister of National Defence made a very clear explanation when this item was first called, but unfortunately he is suffering with a sore throat and his voice does not carry very far. I must say that I heard him with some difficulty even at this short distance. He made a very clear explanation and I am sure that Hansard, which is not very far from him, will have a record of his remarks. If the hon. member will look over those remarks to-morrow morning I am sure they will1 disclose a full explanation.
That is locking the door after the horse has been stolen.

Item agreed to.
General stores-further amount required, $600,000.

Here is another item of the type to which I referred. When the national defence main estimates were before the committee for consideration four months ago we were asked to vote $837,800 for general stores, an amount similar to the amount voted the year before. I submit that when the committee allowed that item to pass without discussion it did so because hon. members believed they were voting the government the same amount as had been voted the year before. We are now being asked to vote almost a duplicate amount and I should like to know what has happened to the general stores in the last few months to necessitate this additional vote of 8600,000.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The same explanation applies so far as the general stores part of this vote is concerned, that is, these stores have been depleted for relief purposes, purchases have not been as heavy as they should be, and it is desirable that they be brought up again to a general average. Included in this item are two others; I referred to one a moment ago, that covering the dominion arsenal. This vote includes an amount of $287,610 to cover the removal of the arsenal from its present dangerous position outside the city walls of Quebec. The filling station is a menace to life and property and preparations have been made to affect a change. Hitherto these preparations have proceeded rather slowly but the buildings at Valcartier
Supply-National Defence

are almost ready to receive the filling station and it is intended to proceed more rapidly with the evacuation of the site at Quebec.
What is the amount of the item referred to by the minister?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence

speechtext: That is included in the $600,000?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes. There is another item for $201,095 under the heading of artillery stores. The number of fuses have been allowed to drop below the quantity required for even peace time practice on the ranges. Of that vote, $125,485 is to provide for training and instructional requirements for the permanent force, non-permanent active militia units and central camps and schools. Wheels, et cetera, to the amount of $40,790 are necessary owing to the mechanization of "C" battery and the increased use of motor transport vehicles for gun hauling. Quick firing three inch equipment is necessary to provide one section of modern armament for defence of Halifax and Esquimalt fortresses. The existing equipment is obsolete and is of little value either for training or for defence purposes. There is not one single antiaircraft gun in Canada and it is impossible to carry on the training of men in the use of these guns.

If what the minister states is correct it offers the strongest reason why he should have told the fact to the committee when the main estimates were under consideration. He states now that this equipment is obsolete making it impossible to give training to the men, but it seems to me he should have brought these facts to the attention of the committee when the main estimates were being considered. I cannot understand why he should leave these items to the last moment and then bring them up in the form of supplementary estimates during the dying days of a parliament.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
I have endeavoured to
give this explanation more than once. As minister for the time being I consider it necessary that these things should be done and the government has decided to proceed this far in agreeing to do wha.t I consider was necessary to be done in the department.

It seems to me that all the minister's explanation amounts to is this: Having charge of the military, naval and aviation services he has been able

to persuade the government to come up to a certain mark in making provision for these services, while the ministers of other departments, for example the Department of Labour and the Department of Agriculture, have not been able to persuade the government to come up to what they believed to be the necessary mark in order to serve the needs which they have particularly in charge. I am still in doubt as to the real reason why the minister has been able to obtain this supremacy over his colleagues in the government.

Will the right hon.
gentleman tell me the item in agriculture to which he refers?
I did not refer to any particular item.

How would the arsenal
at Quebec come under general stores?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I cannot give any reason why it should or should not. The arsenal turns out a certain quantity of small arms munitions as well as shells and fuses, all of which are stores until they are used.

Is this expenditure to be
made on the building?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The expenditure will be
in the transfer to Valcartier of the contents of the arsenal, its machinery and stocks from the dangerous position it occupies outside the citadel in Quebec.

I understand that
this amount of $287,000 in connection with the arsenal is to cover the transfer of a dangerous plant to Valcartier where new quarters have been erected. Do I understand that the sum of $287,000 is simply for the transfer of the present equipment of these buildings to Valcartier, or is it, as I think it is, an allotment of money to the dominion arsenal, Quebec, for the manufacture of a certain number of rounds of ammunition? I think that is what it is. I cannot understand what the minister means by stores, if he is going to use that money for the transfer of the equipment of the buildings from Quebec to Valcartier. It may mean that he is going to buy new machinery, new equipment. The minister's reply was far from clear; perhaps he would elucidate it.

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext:
The removal of the
dominion arsenal from Quebec to its new site at Valcartier is a scheme which has been long considered, which has been started, and which is of considerable magnitude, and it has been

Supply-National Defence
proceeded with as money was available. A certain portion, of the buildings necessary to receive certain portions of the work done in the arsenal are now just about ready at Val-cartier to receive them. That change over, what is known as the filling station, will be made. The most dangerous part of the process will be removed from Quebec to Val-cartier. This money will enable the next piece of development work to go on at Val-cartier, and as it is completed more of the work done in the arsenal at Quebec can be moved over to Valcartier.

Does the minister
mean that the dangerous buildings of our dominion arsenal, which are on the coal fields, are going to be transferred from Quebec to Valcartier?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: Yes.

Then a portion of this $287,000 is to be used to transfer the equipment of these buildings to the new site and also to enable the manufacturing at the new site of a certain amount of ammunition. I suppose that is the proper explanation?

speakerposition: Minister of Fisheries; Minister of National Defence
speechtext: I think the hon. member has now stated it correctly. That is the way I understand it.

Mr. Chairman, if I
remember well, General1 McNaughton has been chief of staff with a salary of $10,000 a year. He was appointed1 to the national research counoil at a salary of $15,000, and no provision was made for his superannuation from his position as chief of staff. If he is not superannuated within a month' or thirty days after he is appointed to a higher salaried position, which appointment has been made, his superannuation will be based, not on the salary of $10,000 which he was receiving as chief of staff, but on the $15,000 which he receives in his present position, which does not carry superannuation. I hope that the minister catches my point. If General McNaughton is superannuated1 now he will be superannuated on the basis of a salary of $10,000, but if he is not superannuated until next week he will be superannuated1 on the basis of a salary of $15,000. May I ask the minister if he has taken any steps for the superannuation of General McNaughton right now in order to save several thousand dollars to the public exchequer, or if he is going to wait to give him a fat superannuation later on this week? Was I clear enough? Here as a case where a man is entitled to superannuation based on a salary of $10,000, and it is time right now
to save several thousand dollars of public money to the public exchequer, and the minister sife idle in his seat and does not answer my question. I ask him, will he superannuate General McNaughton right now on the basis of a salary of $10,000 in order not to give him the privilege of having a superannuation on $15,000 in a position which does not carry any superannuation, according to the statute. No answer? Sir, this is a scandal.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.
Here I denounce this case of favouritism with regard to the chief of staff, and all the ministers sit idle and dumb in their seats. I want an answer.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
The question of
the salary or superannuation of General McNaughton is not under consideration. It has nothing to do with this item.
I heard the Prime Minister state that General McNaughton was not now receiving any salary as chief of staff but was practically acting as chief of staff until he was replaced.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. That would
come under item 330, not 329. When we come to the next item the hon. member may discuss it.
Item agreed to.

No, Mr. Chairman, the item is not carried, because the chief of staff has to look after all these matters that come under item 329, and if you are not satisfied as to that, we will have the statutes brought into this chamber. What I a,m saying is absolutely pertinent to the item before us, and it was because the government was unable to answer that you ruled me out of order. It is a scandal in this house, and a scandal against parliamentary tradition. What does the hon. member for Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon) say? I have been kind to him because we were college mates. Let me tell him what the electors of the province of Quebec think of him.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order.

Can we not invoke free speech here, Mr. Chairman? Are we in Russia that we must stand in silence? This is one scandal in which there has been favouritism for the chief of staff who has been instrumental in having the large salaries that are paid to militia men and to himself, and I have a right to denounce it in this House of Commons.
Progress reported.
Eight Hour Day
What will foe the business for to-morrow?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: Amendments from the Senate. A bill was sent back from this house to the Senate with the statement that we had concurred in all the amendments except one, the consequential one. That appears on the record but not in the report of proceedings in the house. It apparently was overlooked that that was done. We will take the Senate amendments and I think there are two small bills, and then we will continue with supply.
But not take the elections act?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No.
Perhaps we have had enough of elections for to-day?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: No, we are willing and prepared to face another-
Let us have it now.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -just as soon as possible-
